judge.reasoning:
Section relevance is excellent: all five sections map directly to the brief's stated segments — family/child density (kids-eat-free), seniors (senior discount), moderate-income affordability (budget tier), shift-worker employment patterns (extended hours), and county-level target-market scoping. Nothing is off-topic. Tool/metric selection is similarly strong: the agent queried the exact metrics an ideal-customer profile for this diner needs (median household income, income distribution/$150k+ share, under-10 and under-20 shares, married-household share, over-65 and 80+ shares, widowed share, labor force participation, unemployment). The only real gap versus the brief is the near-total absence of the location/logistics criteria the owner explicitly named — proximity to highways, schools, shopping centers, and the $3,000–$5,000 lease budget (commercial rent/real-estate cost) are never analyzed, which is why overall stops at 8 rather than higher; those are decision-critical for actually 'picking a location.'

Narrative quality is specific and actionable: it names concrete ZIPs and counties, ties each demographic back to a menu/program feature (e.g., ~20% senior share justifying senior discounts, married-share anchoring kids-eat-free, participation supporting late-night shift traffic), and even flags high-unemployment 'watch-list' markets requiring cost discipline. It avoids generic filler. Minor deduction: it sometimes overstates precision and slightly editorializes ('lives or dies').

Data plausibility is mostly sound (Ohio suburban incomes $40k–$55k, over-65 shares ~20%, participation 55–67% are all reasonable), but there are internal inconsistencies and a few implausible outliers that hurt this dimension: (1) the summary median_household_income is $48,312 yet Canal Winchester's bubble reuses that exact $48,312 figure while the narrative later cites its own distinct income — a likely copy/placeholder error; (2) Section 5's Putnam County at 0.63% and Mercer at 1.59% unemployment with populations of 2,515 and 738 are implausible and contradict the report's own claim to focus on populous suburbs (these tiny geographies were supposedly excluded); (3) Euclid's population shown as 9,172 is far too low for that suburb (~48k); (4) the summary home_ownership_rate is null. County-vs-ZIP labeling is also muddled (many 'suburban ZIPs' are actually core-city ZIPs like Cleveland 44105, Toledo 43604, Cincinnati 45225).

Visualizations are largely appropriate: bubble charts correctly used for multi-dimensional comparisons (income × participation × population × age), bar charts for categorical ZIP/county comparisons, and a histogram for the labor-force-participation distribution. Small issues: the opportunity bubble is titled 'Income vs. Family Presence' but the y-axis is labor force participation, not a family metric — a title/axis mismatch; and several bar charts show only a truncated 5-item subset, weakening comparison completeness. Overall a genuinely useful, near-presentation-ready report that would be stronger with real-estate/lease and proximity analysis plus cleanup of the data inconsistencies.
